questiontext.text:
Give a counterexample to each conjecture. Give \(\theta\) in degrees, as a number without the \(^\circ\) sign.

  1. For all \(\theta\), \(\cos(-\theta)=-\cos\theta\).

    \(\theta=\) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

  2. For all \(\theta\), \(\sin(2\theta)=2\sin\theta\).

    \(\theta=\) [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

generalfeedback.text:
1. The cosine graph is symmetric about the vertical axis, so \(\cos(-\theta)=\cos\theta\) for every \(\theta\). The conjecture therefore says \(\cos\theta=-\cos\theta\), that is \(\cos\theta=0\), which is true only for \(\theta=90^\circ+180^\circ k\), where \(k\) is an integer. Any other angle is a counterexample. For example, take \(\theta=0^\circ\): \(\cos(-0^\circ)=\cos 0^\circ=1\), but \(-\cos 0^\circ=-1\). Since \(1\neq -1\), the conjecture is false.

  2. The double angle formula gives \(\sin 2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta\). So the conjecture needs \(2\sin\theta\cos\theta=2\sin\theta\), that is \(\sin\theta(\cos\theta-1)=0\), which happens only when \(\sin\theta=0\), that is \(\theta=180^\circ k\). Any other angle is a counterexample. For example, take \(\theta=90^\circ\): \(\sin 180^\circ=0\), but \(2\sin 90^\circ=2\). Since \(0\neq 2\), the conjecture is false.

The unit matters. In radians, \(\theta=90\) is a counterexample to (a), because \(\cos 90\neq 0\) when \(90\) is in radians; but \(90^\circ\) is not a counterexample, because \(\cos 90^\circ=0\).

questionnote.text: Fixed: Exercises 2 and 3, counterexamples in degrees (e.g. 0 and 90).

questiondescription.text: This question is directly adapted from Exercises 2 and 3 in Section 3 (p. 8) of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022.

truefeedback.text: \(\cos(-\theta)=\cos\theta\) for every \(\theta\), so the two sides differ whenever \(\cos\theta\neq 0\), as it is at \(\theta={@t2@}^\circ\).[[if test='showc']] Here \(\cos(-\theta)={@cv2@}\) and \(-\cos\theta={@-cv2@}\).[[/if]]

falsefeedback.text: At \(\theta={@t2@}^\circ\), \(\cos\theta=0\), so \(\cos(-\theta)=0\) and \(-\cos\theta=0\): the two sides are equal, and the conjecture is true for this \(\theta\). This is not a counterexample: a false conjecture can still be true at some angles. Try a different angle, and work out both sides.

truefeedback.text: \(\sin 2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta\), which equals \(2\sin\theta\) only when \(\sin\theta=0\). At \(\theta={@t3@}^\circ\) it is not.[[if test='shows']] Here \(\sin 2\theta={@sv2@}\) and \(2\sin\theta={@sv1@}\).[[/if]]

falsefeedback.text: At \(\theta={@t3@}^\circ\), \(\sin\theta=0\), so \(\sin 2\theta=0\) and \(2\sin\theta=0\): the two sides are equal, and the conjecture is true for this \(\theta\). This is not a counterexample: a false conjecture can still be true at some angles. Try a different angle, and work out both sides.
